newsitem.title: USA: Albright divides world states into four categories.
newsitem.headline: Albright divides world states into four categories.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright gave a glimpse of her world view on Friday, saying she put countries in four categories -- law-abiding states, emerging states, rogue states and failed states.

Albright, introducing herself at a wide-ranging first news conference at the State Department one day after being sworn in to office, said she had asked herself what should be the ultimate goals of U.S. policy.

The fundamental aim, she said, was to ensure that "the American people are safe, secure, and prosperous, and are able to operate within a safe, secure and prosperous world, which means that the more democracies and market economies that exist, the better it is for Americans."
The framework for that was "a functioning international system," she said, and divided the world's states into four categories. They were:
-- Those that "see the advantages of a functioning international system, who understand the rules, who know that a rule of law system works..." This was the largest group, she said.
-- Evolving democracies that "would very much like to be a part of an international system and obey the rules, but may not have all the resources yet to fully participate in it."
-- "Rogue states," which "not only do not see an advantage to a functioning international system, but ... feel that they are more important when they can disrupt the international system."
The long-term U.S. aim was to get every state into the first category, she said.
Albright did not list countries in each category, mentioning only in response to a later question that Iraq and Iran were "rogues".

Washington would "look at the rogues case by case but basically have them understand -- because they are being isolated ... that they need to change their behaviour in order to be able to benefit from the international system."
For those in the fourth category, she said the goal would be "to make the failed states not wards of the system."
